explanation:
# Vacation days by seniority in Argentina (LCT Art. 150)

Paid vacation is a non-waivable labor right in Argentina, regulated by Law No. 20,744 — the LCT (*Ley de Contrato de Trabajo*, Argentina's Labor Contract Law, the country's core employment statute). This calculator determines the vacation days you're entitled to based on your seniority, following the mandatory minimums of **Article 150 of the LCT**.

---

## How your vacation is calculated

The LCT sets a progressive scale based on the **years of continuous or non-continuous seniority** accumulated with the same employer as of **December 31** of the year the vacation corresponds to. In other words, seniority is "snapshotted" at year-end, not at the moment you actually take the days.

### Days-worked requirement

To be entitled to the full period, you must have worked **at least half of the working days in the year**. If you worked less (for example, you started in July), you earn **1 vacation day for every 20 days worked** that year. This is known as the proportional period.

### Vacation scale by seniority

| Seniority | Calendar days of vacation |
|---|---|
| Less than 5 years | 14 days |
| 5 to less than 10 years | 21 days |
| 10 to less than 20 years | 28 days |
| 20 years or more | 35 days |

> **Important:** the days are **calendar days** (they include Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays), not working days. 14 calendar days roughly equal 10 working days.

---

## When and how vacation is taken

- **Standard period:** between October 1 and April 30 of the following year. Outside that window, the employer may grant it only with the employee's agreement.
- **Advance notice:** the employer must notify the start date at least **45 days in advance**.
- **Advance payment:** vacation pay must be paid **before** the leave begins, not at the end.
- **Splitting:** the period can be divided into two parts, as long as one of them is not shorter than the legal minimums (Art. 164 LCT).
- **Carryover:** up to **50% of the period** can be carried over to the following year, by agreement between the parties.

---

## How vacation pay is calculated

The amount you receive during vacation is not simply the monthly salary divided by 30. The legal formula (Art. 155 LCT) is:

**Daily pay = Monthly salary ÷ 25**

That daily value is then multiplied by the number of vacation days you're entitled to. The divisor of **25** (rather than 30) makes the vacation amount slightly higher than the monthly pro-rata — compensation for the consecutive nature of the days.

---

## What this calculator does NOT include

- **Collective bargaining agreements (CCTs):** many sectors have scales more favorable than the LCT (teachers, bank employees, hospitality workers, etc.). This calculation reflects only the legal minimum; always check the agreement that applies to you.
- **Proportional vacation on termination:** if you leave the company before taking vacation, you're entitled to payment for the days proportional to the time worked that year. That case requires a specific calculation.
- **Domestic workers:** they're governed by Law 26,844 and follow a different scale.
- **Public administration employees:** the applicable sector-level agreement or jurisdiction-specific rules apply instead.
- **Overtime and variable pay:** the calculation base may change if you earn variable compensation.

---

## Common mistakes

**❌ Counting working days instead of calendar days**
The 14, 21, 28, or 35 days are calendar days. If your vacation starts on a Monday, the count runs from that day and includes the weekend.

**❌ Measuring seniority at today's date**
Seniority is determined as of December 31 of the corresponding year, not when the leave begins.

**❌ Assuming vacation pay equals the regular monthly salary**
The calculation uses a divisor of 25, which generally results in a slightly higher amount than the calendar-day pro-rata.

**❌ Forgetting the days-worked requirement**
Someone who joined mid-year doesn't get the full period, but proportional days instead (1 day per 20 days worked).

---

## Relevant legal context

LCT No. 20,744 has been in force since 1976, with later amendments. The key articles for vacation are:
- **Art. 150:** day scale by seniority
- **Art. 151:** days-worked requirement and proportional calculation
- **Art. 154:** granting period
- **Art. 155:** pay during vacation
- **Art. 162:** vacation and contract termination

---

*This calculation is indicative and reflects the LCT minimums in force as of 2026. For specific situations (applicable collective agreement, dismissals, part-time work, or multiple jobs), consult an HR professional or an employment lawyer.*

faq.q: What law governs vacation days in Argentina?
faq.a: Argentina's Labor Contract Law (LCT) 20.744, Articles 150-157, establishes mandatory vacation day minimums.

faq.q: What's the vacation day scale by years of service?
faq.a: Up to 5 years: 14 days; 5-10 years: 21 days; 10-20 years: 28 days; 20+ years: 35 days.

faq.q: How are vacation days calculated in the first year?
faq.a: If you haven't completed 6 months of employment, you earn 1 day per month worked (pro-rata basis).

faq.q: Are vacation days calendar days or working days?
faq.a: They are calendar days, including weekends and holidays.

faq.q: When can I take my vacation days?
faq.a: The standard vacation period is October-April, but employers and employees can negotiate alternative dates.

faq.q: Can I sell or waive my unused vacation days?
faq.a: No. Vacation time is a non-waivable right under Argentine law.

faq.q: Can I accumulate vacation days to the next year?
faq.a: Yes, you can accumulate up to 50% of your annual entitlement to the following year.

faq.q: What if I leave my job? Do I get paid for unused vacation?
faq.a: Yes. Unused vacation days must be paid out at your regular salary rate when employment ends.

faq.q: How is vacation calculated for part-time employees?
faq.a: Part-time workers receive proportional vacation days based on their hours worked.
